title: Random Signals through LTI Systems
description: What filters do to noise: output mean and PSD, output power and noise-equivalent bandwidth, thermal and kT/C noise, and better SNR by filtering.

study.title: The mean at the output
study.body: When a WSS process $X(t)$ drives a stable LTI system with impulse response $h(t)$ and frequency response $H(f)$, the output $Y(t)$ is WSS too. Its mean is the input mean times the DC gain: a DC level passes like any DC signal, and a high-pass or band-pass filter ($H(0) = 0$) removes it completely.

study.title: Output PSD and power
study.body: The output PSD is the input PSD shaped by the **power gain** $|H(f)|^2$; the phase of $H$ plays no role. The output power is the area under $S_Y$, and the output autocorrelation is the inverse Fourier transform of $S_Y$. A Gaussian input gives a Gaussian output, and white input noise comes out 'coloured': correlated over roughly the length of the impulse response.

study.title: Noise-equivalent bandwidth
study.body: For white input noise, $P_Y = \frac{N_0}{2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|H(f)|^2df$. Write this as $N_0|H(0)|^2B_N$: the **noise-equivalent bandwidth** $B_N$ is the width of the ideal low-pass filter (same peak gain) that passes the same noise power. A first-order RC low-pass with $f_c = 1/(2\pi RC)$ has $B_N = \frac{\pi}{2}f_c = \frac{1}{4RC}$, 57 % more than $f_c$; a second-order Butterworth has $1.11f_c$.

study.title: White noise through an RC low-pass
study.body: White noise with $N_0/2 = 10^{-15}$ V²/Hz (two-sided) drives an RC low-pass. The output PSD follows the input up to $f_c$ and then falls at 20 dB/decade. The output power $N_0B_N = \frac{N_0}{2}\pi f_c$ is proportional to $f_c$, so the rms noise grows with $\sqrt{f_c}$. Drag $f_c$.

study.title: Thermal noise and kT/C
study.body: A resistor at temperature $T$ has an open-circuit noise voltage with one-sided PSD $4kTR$ (two-sided $2kTR$), so a bandwidth $B$ holds $\sqrt{4kTRB}$ rms, with $k = 1.38\times10^{-23}$ J/K. With a capacitor across it, the RC low-pass limits the noise bandwidth to $B_N = 1/(4RC)$, so $\overline{v_C^2} = 4kTR\cdot\frac{1}{4RC} = kT/C$, independent of $R$: a larger $R$ is noisier but narrows the band by the same factor. This sets the noise floor of every sample-and-hold and switched-capacitor circuit (300 K below).

study.title: Filtering improves the SNR
study.body: A slowly varying signal sits in white noise. A low-pass filter passes the signal almost unchanged, but the noise power is proportional to the noise bandwidth. Cutting $B_N$ from $B_1$ to $B_2$ (still wider than the signal band) improves the SNR by the factor $B_1/B_2$, i.e. $10\log(B_1/B_2)$ dB. The best filter for a known pulse shape, the matched filter, follows in the next unit.

study.title: Worked example: output autocorrelation of an RC filter
study.body: White noise $N_0/2$ through an RC low-pass gives $S_Y(f) = \frac{N_0/2}{1 + (2\pi fRC)^2}$, whose inverse transform is $R_Y(\tau)$ below. Check: $R_Y(0) = N_0/(4RC) = N_0B_N$. Samples more than a few $RC$ apart are nearly uncorrelated: the filter's memory sets the correlation time. Example: $R$ = 10 kΩ and $C$ = 10 nF give $RC$ = 100 µs and $B_N$ = 2.5 kHz; samples 230 µs apart still have a correlation coefficient of $e^{-2.3}$ = 0.1.

lessons.title: Mean, PSD and power at the output

steps.title: What a filter does to a random signal
steps.body: A stable LTI system turns a WSS input into a WSS output. The mean is multiplied by the DC gain $H(0)$, and the PSD by the power gain $|H(f)|^2$.

steps.prompt: A noisy DC voltage with mean {{mu|V}} passes through a coupling capacitor, i.e. a high-pass filter $H(f) = \frac{jf/f_c}{1 + jf/f_c}$. What is the mean of the output?
steps.explanation: $m_Y = H(0)\,m_X$, and a high-pass has $H(0) = 0$: the capacitor blocks DC, and only the fluctuations (above $f_c$) pass.

steps.prompt: White noise with a two-sided PSD of ${{m}}\times10^{-11}$ V²/Hz plus a DC level of {{mu|V}} drives an amplifier with $H(f) = \frac{K}{1 + jf/f_c}$, $K$ = {{K}}, $f_c$ = {{fc|Hz}}.

ask.prompt: What is the mean of the output?
What is the output PSD at $f$ = {{f|Hz}}, in V²/Hz?

steps.title: Noise-equivalent bandwidth
steps.body: For white input noise ($N_0/2$, two-sided), the output power is $N_0|H(0)|^2B_N$, where $B_N$ is the width of the brick-wall low-pass that passes the same noise power (equal areas under $|H|^2$). A first-order RC low-pass has $B_N = \frac{\pi}{2}f_c = \frac{1}{4RC}$.

steps.prompt: White noise with a two-sided PSD of ${{m}}\times10^{-15}$ V²/Hz drives an RC low-pass filter with $f_c$ = {{fc|Hz}}. What is the rms output noise voltage?
What is the noise-equivalent bandwidth of a first-order RC low-pass filter with $f_c$ = {{fc|Hz}}?
steps.explanation: $B_N = \int_0^\infty\frac{df}{1 + (f/f_c)^2} = f_c\arctan(\infty) = \frac{\pi}{2}f_c$ = **{{pi/2*fc|Hz}}**: the slow 20 dB/decade roll-off lets noise above $f_c$ through. $\pi f_c$ would integrate over negative frequencies too, and $2\pi f_c$ mixes up Hz and rad/s.

steps.title: Thermal noise and kT/C
steps.body: A resistor's open-circuit noise voltage has a one-sided PSD of $4kTR$, so a bandwidth $B$ holds $\sqrt{4kTRB}$ rms ($k = 1.38\times10^{-23}$ J/K). Across a capacitor, the RC low-pass limits the noise bandwidth to $B_N = 1/(4RC)$, which gives $kT/C$, independent of $R$.

steps.prompt: A {{C|F}} sampling capacitor at 300 K is charged through a switch with some on-resistance. What is the rms kT/C noise voltage on the capacitor?
steps.explanation: $V_n = \sqrt{kT/C}$ with $kT = 1.38\times10^{-23}\cdot300 = 4.14\times10^{-21}$ J and $C$ = {{C|F}}: **{{sqrt(1.38e-23*300/C)|V}}**, whatever the switch resistance.

steps.prompt: A resistor $R$ has a capacitor $C$ across it, and the resistor's thermal noise is the only noise source. Increasing $R$ increases the rms noise voltage across the capacitor.
steps.explanation: The noise PSD $4kTR$ grows with $R$, but the noise bandwidth $1/(4RC)$ shrinks by the same factor: $\overline{v^2} = 4kTR \cdot \frac{1}{4RC} = kT/C$. Only a larger capacitor (or a lower temperature) reduces it.

steps.prompt: What is the rms thermal noise voltage of a {{R|Ω}} resistor at {{T}} K, measured in a brick-wall bandwidth of {{B|Hz}}?

steps.title: Filtering improves the SNR
steps.body: A slowly varying signal passes a low-pass filter almost unchanged, but the white-noise power at the output is proportional to the noise bandwidth $B_N$. Reducing $B_N$ from $B_1$ to $B_2$ (still wider than the signal) therefore improves the SNR by $B_1/B_2$.

steps.prompt: A sensor signal with all its content below 50 Hz is measured in white noise with a noise bandwidth of {{Bw|Hz}}, giving an SNR of {{SNR0}} dB. A low-pass filter reduces the noise bandwidth to {{B|Hz}} without affecting the signal.

ask.prompt: By how many dB does the SNR improve?
ask.explanation: The noise power drops by $B_1/B_2$ = {{Bw/B}}; the signal is unchanged. Improvement: 10 log({{Bw/B}}) = **{{10*log10(Bw/B)||3}} dB**.

ask.prompt: What is the new SNR, in dB?

steps.title: White noise through an RC low-pass
steps.body: White noise with $N_0/2 = 10^{-15}$ V²/Hz (two-sided) drives an RC low-pass. The output PSD equals the input PSD up to $f_c$ and then falls at 20 dB/decade; the output power is $\frac{N_0}{2}\pi f_c$. Drag $f_c$ and watch the rms noise grow with $\sqrt{f_c}$.

steps.prompt: White noise with a two-sided PSD of ${{m}}\times10^{-15}$ V²/Hz drives an RC low-pass. Set $f_c$ so that the rms output noise is {{Vt|V}}.
White noise with a two-sided PSD of ${{m}}\times10^{-14}$ V²/Hz drives an RC low-pass with $R$ = {{R|Ω}} and $C$ = {{C|F}}. The output autocorrelation is $R_Y(\tau) = \frac{N_0}{4RC}e^{-|\tau|/RC}$.

ask.prompt: What is the output power $R_Y(0)$, in V²?
What is the correlation coefficient of output samples taken {{k*R*C|s}} apart?
ask.explanation: $\rho(\tau) = R_Y(\tau)/R_Y(0) = e^{-\tau/RC}$ = $e^{-{{k}}}$ = **{{exp(-k)}}**: the filter's time constant {{R*C|s}} sets the correlation time.

steps.prompt: Three low-pass filters have the same peak gain and the same 3 dB frequency $f_c$. White noise drives each of them. Which output contains the most noise power?
steps.explanation: Their noise-equivalent bandwidths are $1.571f_c$ (RC), $1.111f_c$ (second-order Butterworth) and exactly $f_c$ (brick wall). The gentle 20 dB/decade roll-off of the RC filter lets the most noise through above $f_c$; steeper filters approach $B_N = f_c$.

steps.prompt: Halving the noise-equivalent bandwidth (without touching the signal) improves the SNR of a slowly varying signal in white noise by 3 dB.
steps.explanation: The noise power $N_0B_N$ halves while the signal power stays: SNR × 2, i.e. +3.01 dB. The rms noise voltage drops by only $\sqrt2$.

steps.prompt: A digital filter averages the last {{N}} samples: $y[n] = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}x[n-k]$. The input samples are independent with mean {{mu|V}} and standard deviation {{sig|V}}.

ask.prompt: What is the mean of the output?
ask.explanation: The DC gain is $H(0) = \sum_k h[k] = N \cdot \frac1N = 1$, so $m_Y = m_X$ = **{{mu|V}}**.

ask.prompt: What is the standard deviation of the output?
ask.explanation: For white input, $\sigma_Y^2 = \sigma_X^2\sum_k h[k]^2 = \sigma_X^2 \cdot N \cdot \frac{1}{N^2} = \sigma_X^2/N$. So $\sigma_Y$ = {{sig|V}}/√{{N}} = **{{sig/sqrt(N)|V}}**.

steps.prompt: A {{N}}-bit ADC has a full-scale range of {{V|V}}. Its sample-and-hold capacitor must keep the kT/C noise at 300 K below half an LSB rms. What is the smallest allowed capacitance?
steps.explanation: LSB = $V_{FS}/2^{{{N}}}$ = {{V/2^N|V}}, so the limit is {{V/2^N/2|V}}. $\sqrt{kT/C} \le$ {{V/2^N/2|V}} ⇒ $C \ge \frac{kT}{(\text{LSB}/2)^2} = \frac{4.14\times10^{-21}}{({{V/2^N/2*1e6}}\ \mu\text{V})^2}$ = **{{1.38e-23*300/(V/2^N/2)^2*1e12}} pF**. Each extra bit needs 4× the capacitance.

steps.prompt: A sensor delivers a DC level of {{mu|V}} plus white noise with a two-sided PSD of ${{m}}\times10^{-16}$ V²/Hz to an amplifier with $H(f) = \frac{K}{1 + jf/f_c}$, $K$ = {{K}}, $f_c$ = {{fc|Hz}}.

ask.prompt: What is the rms noise at the output?
ask.explanation: $P_n = N_0|H(0)|^2B_N = 2S \cdot K^2 \cdot \frac{\pi}{2}f_c$ = {{K^2*S*pi*fc}} V², so the rms noise is **{{K*sqrt(S*pi*fc)|V}}**.

ask.prompt: What is the output signal-to-noise ratio (DC power over noise power), in dB?
ask.explanation: DC power: $(Km_X)^2$ = ({{K*mu|V}})² = {{(K*mu)^2}} V². Noise power: $K^2\cdot2S\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}f_c$ = {{K^2*S*pi*fc}} V². SNR = 10 log({{(K*mu)^2}}/{{K^2*S*pi*fc}}) = **{{10*log10(mu^2/(S*pi*fc))||3}} dB**. The power gain $K^2$ multiplies signal and noise alike, so it cancels: the SNR is set by the input level, the noise density and the noise bandwidth.

steps.prompt: A single-tuned LC band-pass with centre frequency {{f0|Hz}} and 3 dB bandwidth $BW$ = {{BW|Hz}} has $|H(f)|^2 \approx \frac{1}{1 + [2(f - f_0)/BW]^2}$ near $f_0$ (peak gain 1). White noise with a two-sided PSD of ${{m}}\times10^{-16}$ V²/Hz drives it.

ask.explanation: The resonance curve has the same shape as an RC low-pass with $f_c = BW/2$ on each side of $f_0$: $B_N = \int\frac{df}{1 + [2(f - f_0)/BW]^2} = \frac{\pi}{2}BW$ = **{{pi/2*BW|Hz}}**.

ask.prompt: What is the rms output noise voltage?
ask.explanation: $P = N_0B_N = 2S\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}BW = {{m*pi*BW/10000||3}}\times10^{-12}$ V² (the passbands at $\pm f_0$ together), so $V_{rms}$ = **{{sqrt(S*pi*BW)|V}}**.

steps.prompt: Noise is white up to {{Bw|Hz}} (a brick-wall limit). Adding an RC low-pass with $f_c$ = {{fc|Hz}} (well below {{Bw|Hz}}) leaves the slow signal unaffected. By how many dB does the SNR improve?
steps.explanation: Noise bandwidth before: {{Bw|Hz}}; after: $B_N \approx \frac{\pi}{2}f_c$ = {{pi/2*fc|Hz}} (since $f_c \ll$ {{Bw|Hz}}). Improvement: 10 log({{Bw|Hz}} / {{pi/2*fc|Hz}}) = **{{10*log10(Bw/(pi/2*fc))||3}} dB**.

steps.prompt: White Gaussian noise passed through an LTI filter is still Gaussian, but no longer white.
steps.explanation: Each output value is a weighted sum (integral) of Gaussian input values, so it is Gaussian. The PSD, however, is reshaped to $|H(f)|^2N_0/2$, and the output samples are correlated over roughly the length of the impulse response.

steps.prompt: A {{R|Ω}} resistor at 300 K has a capacitor $C$ = {{C|F}} across it. What is the rms noise voltage across $C$ in the band from 0 up to the corner frequency $f_c = 1/(2\pi RC)$ only?
steps.explanation: $\int_0^{f_c}\frac{4kTR}{1 + (f/f_c)^2}df = 4kTRf_c\arctan(1) = \pi kTRf_c = \frac{kT}{2C}$: exactly half of the total $kT/C$ lies below the corner. With $kT = 4.14\times10^{-21}$ J and $C$ = {{C|F}}: $V = \sqrt{kT/2C}$ = **{{sqrt(1.38e-23*300/(2*C))|V}}**.

steps.prompt: White noise is filtered by an RC low-pass with $R$ = {{R|Ω}} and $C$ = {{C|F}}. How far apart must output samples be for their correlation coefficient to drop to {{c}}?
A noise voltage with $R_X(\tau) = {{P}}\,e^{-{{a}}|\tau|}$ V² drives an RC low-pass with $f_c$ = {{fc|Hz}}. What is the output power, in V²?
steps.explanation: With $\omega_c = 2\pi f_c$ = {{2*pi*fc}} rad/s: $P_Y = \int\frac{2aP}{a^2+\omega^2}\cdot\frac{\omega_c^2}{\omega_c^2+\omega^2}\frac{d\omega}{2\pi} = P\,\frac{\omega_c}{a + \omega_c}$ = {{P}} × {{2*pi*fc}}/({{a}} + {{2*pi*fc}}) = **{{P*2*pi*fc/(a+2*pi*fc)}}** V². A filter much wider than the noise ($\omega_c \gg a$) passes nearly all of it.

steps.prompt: A sinusoid is received in white noise with a two-sided PSD of ${{m}}\times10^{-16}$ V²/Hz. The receiver's band-pass filter has a noise bandwidth of {{BN|Hz}}. What sinusoid amplitude gives an output SNR of {{SNRdB}} dB?
steps.explanation: Noise power $N_0B_N = 2\cdot{{m}}\times10^{-16}\cdot{{BN}} = {{2*m*BN/10000||3}}\times10^{-12}$ V². Required signal power $A^2/2$ = {{10^(SNRdB/10)}} times that, so $A = \sqrt{2 \cdot \mathrm{SNR} \cdot N_0B_N}$ = **{{sqrt(2*10^(SNRdB/10)*2*S*BN)|V}}**.

steps.prompt: An integrate-and-dump circuit outputs the average of its input over the last $T$ = {{T|s}}: $h(t) = 1/T$ for $0 \le t \le T$, so $|H(f)|^2 = \mathrm{sinc}^2(fT)$. The input is white noise with a two-sided PSD of {{S}} V²/Hz.

ask.prompt: What is the rms output noise?
ask.explanation: $P = N_0B_N = 2S\cdot\frac{1}{2T} = S/T$ = {{S/T}} V², so $V_{rms}$ = **{{sqrt(S/T)|V}}**. Averaging longer reduces the noise as $1/\sqrt{T}$.

steps.prompt: A sensor delivers a DC level of {{mu|V}} in white noise with a two-sided PSD of $10^{-14}$ V²/Hz. An RC low-pass passes the DC unchanged. Set $f_c$ for an output SNR ($\mu^2$ over noise power) of {{SNRdB}} dB.
steps.explanation: Noise power $\frac{N_0}{2}\pi f_c$, so $\mathrm{SNR} = \frac{\mu^2}{\pi f_c N_0/2}$ ⇒ $f_c = \frac{\mu^2}{\pi\cdot10^{-14}\cdot\mathrm{SNR}}$ with $\mu$ = {{mu|V}} and SNR = {{10^(SNRdB/10)}}: **{{ft|Hz}}**.

steps.prompt: A sample-and-hold stores a signal of {{Vs|V}} rms on a {{C|F}} capacitor at 300 K. What is the signal-to-noise ratio set by the kT/C noise, in dB?
For white input noise, the output noise power of a filter depends only on the magnitude response $|H(f)|$, not on its phase response.
steps.explanation: $S_Y(f) = |H(f)|^2S_X(f)$ contains only the magnitude. An all-pass filter changes the waveform of the noise, not its power; this holds for any input PSD, not just white noise.
